1:
Ellicott opens with the question of where the chapter came from, and answers in a way that cuts against the criticism of his own day. The episode derives either from Canaanite records or, as Sayce thinks, from Babylonian ones, and the latter is made more probable by two features: that Amraphel, though but a subject king, is placed first, and that the patriarch is called Abram the Hebrew, which suggests a narrative of foreign origin. Then the concession and the argument built on it: the narrative is Jehovistic, since Abram calls God Jehovah El Elyon, but of such ancient date as to forbid the theory that the occurrence of that name proves later authorship.

Who Amraphel was nobody can say, and Gill sets out the possibilities in descending confidence: Nimrod himself, as the Jewish writers generally say; more likely Ninyas, grandson of Nimrod; or rather some petty prince under the king of Babylon, since though named first he fought under the king of Elam. Then he doubts the framework itself, suggesting the stories told of Ninus and Semiramis may be mere fables, and arguing from silence that Scripture says nothing of Babylon from this point until Merodach Baladan, nor of Assyria until Pul, so it is greatly to be questioned whether those kingdoms rose to any height before then. Keil is candid about what cannot be settled: Ellasar cannot be determined, Knobel supposing it Artemita in southern Assyria; and Goyim is not nations generally but one particular nation, in Delitzsch's opinion an older name for Galilee. Keil adds that five kings in five cities was quite in harmony with the condition of Canaan, where even later every city had its king.

Henry, and Wesley after him almost word for word, observe that this is the first war we read of in scripture, and that though the wars of the nations make the greatest figure in history we should not have had this one at all but for Abram and Lot. Both take the invaders to be not the sovereign princes of Chaldea and Persia but heads of colonies settled near Sodom, retaining the names of the countries they came from. Henry alone stops over the fifth king, unnamed where four are named, and offers two reasons: either he was much more inconsiderable, or much more wicked and inglorious than the rest, and worthy to be forgotten. On the twelve years he draws the moral that small joy they had of their fruitful land while tributaries to a foreign power, unable to call what they had their own, since rich countries are a desirable prey.

Gill and Wesley both find Noah's prophecy beginning to work here, Chedorlaomer of Elam being of the race of Shem and the kings of the plain of Ham in the line of Canaan, so that Canaan serves Shem; and Gill supplies a legal frame, that Canaan had by violence seized the part of the earth allotted to Shem's sons, so Chedorlaomer claimed his right. Ellicott makes it concrete: the service was a yearly tribute paid for exemption from marauding expeditions, so there must have been envoys going to and from the Jordan valley and Shinar. Calvin looks past the politics and gives three reasons the history is worth remembering: that Lot's gentle reproof found the men of Sodom unteachable, he himself being scourged for having been allured by the rich soil into mixing with wicked men; that God raised up Abram as avenger and liberator, preserving for one man's sake many utterly unworthy; and that Abram was blessed by Melchizedek, in whose person the kingdom and priesthood of Christ was shadowed forth. Clarke contributes the summary of the whole chapter, his one substantive note being chronological: the revolt fell in the thirteenth year, the punitive campaign in the fourteenth.
5:
The campaign runs through a gazetteer of vanished peoples, and the grammarians differ over the first. Keil is minimal and firm: all that is known with certainty of the Rephaim is that they were a tribe of gigantic stature, spread in Abram's time over Peraea, later expelled by the descendants of Lot and by the Amorites and so nearly exterminated that Og of Bashan is called their remnant. Ellicott traces them far more widely — in Bashan, across Jordan in Mount Ephraim, west of Jerusalem, even among the Philistines — and draws the opposite conclusion from the same evidence: in many of those places the word is wrongly translated giants, and so wide a dispersion shows they were among the land's earlier settlers, only their rulers being Amorite. On the Zuzim, Clarke says they are nowhere else spoken of unless they were the Zamzummim, as some imagine; Ellicott treats the identification as settled and makes them an inferior branch of the Rephaim.

Ellicott is the one who supplies religion and archaeology. Ashteroth Karnaim he explains as the two-horned Astarte, the Phoenician Venus, identified by the Rephaim with the moon and introduced by the Amorites; the city was Og's capital, is called the house of Astarte elsewhere, and its remains have been found in the Hauran. The Horites he calls cave-men, the aboriginal inhabitants of Mount Seir afterwards conquered by the Edomites, and points to the miserable condition of these earth-men described in Job; El-paran he takes as a forest of oaks on the edge of the great wilderness, within three days' journey of Sinai. Gill and Clarke agree on the Horites' fate without the colour: they held Seir until Esau's sons drove them out.

Why the well was called the fountain of judgment is disputed three ways. Clarke derives it from the judgment pronounced on Moses and Aaron for their rebellion there. Gill reports the same view from Jarchi and the Targum of Jonathan and rejects it, holding this was the ancient name of the place and the one it bore at the time, as Kadesh was its name when Moses wrote. Ellicott offers a third origin altogether, that at this spring the ancient inhabitants used to meet to settle their disputes. He and Keil converge independently on the site, both pointing to a spring in the same district, Keil crediting its discovery to Rowland and Ellicott to Palmer,. On Hazezon-tamar both agree it is Engedi, Clarke noting from the Song that it was fruitful, Ellicott dwelling on its strategic value.

Two smaller readings part. Ellicott corrects the verb: they did not return but turned, wheeling to the north-west rather than going back by the same route. Gill takes it as genuine doubling back, since having pushed as far as El-paran they had passed by the Amalekites and came back to fall on them. Both Clarke and Keil flag the anachronism in that name, the country being called after Amalek, who was not yet born. On the battle Keil observes that the asphalt pits made the ground unfavourable for flight, so the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fell there while the rest escaped to the Moabitish highlands with their defiles, the conquerors then withdrawing up the Jordan valley toward Damascus. Ellicott draws a geographical inference from the same movement, that since the five kings left their cities to give battle in the vale of Siddim, the vale must embrace a far wider extent of country than the sites of the five cities. Gill explains the sortie by prudence rather than courage: the king of Sodom went out because the enemy was so near that if his men could not stand their ground they might flee to the mountains and not perish in the city. Wesley marks the pause, that after some preparation Chedorlaomer set himself to reduce the revolters.
10:
What the slimepits were is disputed even before the question of how the kings fell into them. Gill takes them for natural fountains, wells casting out bitumen as fountains cast water, so that the place was ready by nature for what it was to become, a bituminous lake named from the Greek word for the pitch; and he cites Brocardus for their being on the shore in his own day, each with pyramids erect which he saw with his own eyes, and reports similar bitumen springs in Greece. Ellicott makes them artificial, holes whence bitumen had been excavated — the natural layers of it, known to the Greeks and Romans as Judean pitch, still existing on the western side of the sea — and notes that such workings are often very deep and would form dangerous impediments in the way of the defeated side.

How the two kings came to fall there is answered four ways, and Calvin canvasses the field before giving his own. Gill has it as a stratagem that recoiled: the kings of the plain chose this vale to fight in and drew up their line here, hoping the enemy would be ignorant of the pits and fall into them and break their ranks. Clarke leaves the sentence open, either that they were defeated on the spot and many slain, or that multitudes perished in the pits; he notes that the Hebrew doubles the word, pits upon pits, meaning a multitude of them, and calls it a bad place to maintain a fight on or to run through in order to escape. Calvin rejects the reading that they blundered in, on the ground that they were by no means ignorant of the neighbouring places and such an accident would rather have befallen foreign enemies; he rejects also the suggestion that they climbed down to preserve their lives; and he concludes that they exchanged one kind of death for another, as men do in desperation, the swords of the enemy being so formidable that they threw themselves headlong in. His argument is from what follows, that those who escaped fled to the mountains, whence we infer that those who took the pits perished: they fell not so much deceived by ignorance of the place as disheartened by fear.

On the sack itself Gill and Clarke agree about the character of the war from opposite starting points. Gill infers it from what the victors did not do — they neither burned the cities nor garrisoned them, which shows them petty princes who came for plunder and for an equivalent for the unpaid tribute. Clarke names the type, a predatory war such as the Arabs carry on to this day, pillaging a city or a caravan and escaping with the booty into the wilderness where pursuit is unsafe and often impossible.

Lot's capture draws the same moral from two men who state it very differently. Calvin first weighs whether he had been compelled to take arms with the rest or remained at home, and since Moses mentions him only at the plundering thinks it probable he was taken at the close of the battle, at home and unarmed; then he draws two lessons, that sufferings are common to the good and the evil, and that the more closely we are connected with the ungodly the more quickly the scourge reaches us when God pours out vengeance on them. Clarke makes the identical point by way of the fable of the geese and the cranes, the geese being found feeding where the cranes were destroying the grain and all taken in the same net — and leaves the application to the reader. Gill adds only that the Jews make Lot fifty years old at this time.
13:
Why Abram is called the Hebrew divides them, and Clarke argues hardest. He derives it from the verb to pass over, from Abram's coming from beyond the Euphrates, and attacks the alternative: many suppose he got the name from Eber, but no one has discovered why he should be named from Eber rather than from his own father, and none of Eber's descendants in six intervening generations was ever called a Hebrew — which he calls a demonstration. Henry holds precisely the view Clarke is demolishing, that Abram is the son and follower of Heber, in whose family the true religion was kept up in a degenerate age, and that he acted here like a Hebrew. Ellicott takes both at once, the immigrant from beyond the river and the patronymic from Eber who had likewise crossed a river,.

Whether a private man might lawfully war on kings is raised only by Calvin, and answered theologically: Abram went endued with the power of the Spirit and guarded by a heavenly command, so did not transgress his vocation, this being his special calling, since he had already been made king of that land though possession was deferred. Gill answers the same difficulty from the law of nations — Lot was only a sojourner in Sodom, with no concern in the quarrel between the kings, so his seizure was unlawful and Abram's arms justified. Henry, with Wesley following him closely, argues from motive: Abram was prompted not by avarice or ambition but purely by charity, and no military expedition was ever finished more honourably. On the messenger, Gill reports two rabbinic identifications — Michael the prince, and Og the last of the giants, come so that Abram might go to war and be killed — and dismisses both as idle fancies; Ellicott makes the noun collective.

The word rendered armed and the word rendered trained are both contested. Calvin objects that the ancient interpreter made the first mean numbered, whereas it signifies to unsheathe or draw out; Ellicott renders it led forth, or literally let them loose, let them pour forth, finding in it both their number and their haste. On trained Calvin denies the military sense and takes it of men brought up under Abram's authority and imbued from childhood with his discipline, who fought the more courageously for his faith. Ellicott affirms the military sense, since Abram's cattle were exposed to the Amalekites, and infers from their number that he was chieftain of a powerful tribe. Wesley takes both senses together, catechized as well as trained, instructed in religion as much as in the art of war, and notes that this was a great family but a small army, about as many as routed the Midianites under Gideon.

How he divided himself is canvassed by Calvin three ways: that Abram alone rushed on with his household, that he and his three confederates divided their bands to strike terror, or that the phrase is a Hebraism for charging into the enemy's midst. He takes the second, because the attack was by night, and ascribes the feat to Abram's faith rather than to the bravery profane history also records. Gill guesses at four divisions under four leaders, to fall on the camp in its four quarters and make a show of a greater army, citing Josephus that the enemy were asleep or drunk. Keil simply summarises the sequence through to the meeting in the king's dale. Clarke twice supplies what the others leave out: that Abram risked his life for the nephew who had lately taken the best of the land and left him what he did not think worth accepting, since a generous mind not only forgives but forgets offences; and that the historian mentions the women with peculiar tenderness, since every reader must be in pain for wives and daughters fallen to a licentious soldiery — yet all were recovered.
17:
Who Melchizedek was is canvassed by five and settled by three. The identification with Shem is reported by Gill, Henry, Wesley and Ellicott, and rejected by all but Wesley. Henry asks two questions of it: why should his name be changed, and how came he to settle in Canaan? Gill adds three: that he should reign in a country possessed by his brother's son, that he should congratulate Abram on the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, one of his own descendants, and above all that a man whose pedigree is famous cannot be called without father or mother. Ellicott explains the motive behind the tradition rather than the tradition itself: so venerable a figure was identified with Shem to reconcile the Jews to his superiority over their forefather. The second candidate, an appearance of the Son of God, is stated by Henry with some sympathy, since it is hard to imagine any mere man described as he is; Gill answers in a line, that he is manifestly distinguished from Christ in the epistle. Wesley alone refuses to choose, since nothing is expressly revealed and we can determine nothing. Clarke, Gill and Ellicott converge on a real man: Clarke dismisses a thousand idle stories and holds him as real a personage as Bera or Birsha, Gill follows Josephus in making him a Canaanite prince raised up by God whose genealogy was kept secret so that he might be a type, and Ellicott makes him king of some Semitic race still occupying Salem.

The bread and wine produce the sharpest exchange. Clarke will have it that they were certainly to refresh Abram and his men, exhausted with the battle and the journey, and not in the way of sacrifice — a conjecture he calls idle. Wesley divides the act by the office: the bread and wine he brought as a king, and as priest he blessed Abram, which we may suppose was the greater refreshment of the two.

Calvin builds the weight of the passage on the blessing, and states the argument twice. Unless the two clauses cohere — that he was the priest of God and that he blessed — nothing uncommon is related, since men bless each other every day; but here a priest of God sanctifies one inferior and subject to himself, and would never have dared bless Abram unless he knew he excelled him in this. He anticipates the reply that Melchizedek did it as a priest by asking whether Abram was not a priest too, and concludes that God had constituted Melchizedek the only head of the whole Church, the truth of the figure being exhibited when Christ blessed the apostles at his ascension. Ellicott, uninterested in either, notes that the word for possessor is literally creator or framer, a poetical word as are those for delivered and enemies, and that the blessing runs in parallel clauses.

Who paid the tithes to whom Calvin has to argue, since some understand they were given to Abram; he answers from Hebrews 7, adding that the reading is absurd anyway, since a priest of God should receive tithes rather than give them. He concludes that the Levitical priesthood is figured here as subordinate to Christ's, and admits he cannot settle whether the tenth was of the spoils or of Abram's own goods. Wesley divides it the same way, a gratuity returned for the king's respects and an offering to God put into his priest's hands, and closes with the application that Christ our great Melchizedek is to be acknowledged as king and priest, and not the tithe of all but all we have given up to him. Clarke supplies the comparative note, that almost all nations of the earth have agreed in devoting a tenth to religious uses. Clarke and Keil agree that the king of Sodom here must be a successor, the former having fallen in the battle.
21:
How generous the king of Sodom's offer was they do not agree. Henry and Wesley take it at face value as gratitude, both preferring the Hebrew reading give me the soul and take thou the substance, and Henry adds a legal reflection: the king had an original right to persons and goods alike, and whether Abram's acquired right by rescue superseded that title would bear a debate, so where a right is dubious it is wisdom to compound the matter by mutual concessions rather than contend. Ellicott quietly removes the generosity by supplying the custom: to this day among the Arabs a man who recovers plundered booty gives up only the persons and keeps the rest, so the king proposed the ordinary rule, and it is Abram who departs from it by accepting nothing. Calvin is harder still. Gratitude to a man would have been commendable had the king not been ungrateful to God, by whose severity and clemency alike he remained unprofited; and it is even possible that a man stripped of everything was using a servile affectation of modesty to gain Abram's favour by asking only for the captives and the empty city. His evidence is what follows later, the men of Sodom vexing righteous Lot in proud forgetfulness of the benefit.

The lifted hand is taken two ways. Clarke makes it the primitive mode of appealing to God, which he supposes obtained among the faithful until circumcision was established as the covenant's sign, after which the hand was often placed instead on the circumcised part. Calvin reads its direction: raising the hand toward heaven declares that we appeal to God as witness and equally as avenger if we break the oath — and he distinguishes it from the raised hands of voting, whence the Greeks derived their word for decreeing. Calvin alone is uneasy that Abram swore at all, since reverence for God's name should make us use it sparingly and only from necessity.

On the proverb itself Gill and Clarke construct it out of different objects. Gill takes the thread as one used in sewing, or else a hair lace of the head, so that with the shoelatchet at the other end the phrase means nothing of his from head to foot. Clarke calls it certainly proverbial and its full meaning perhaps unknown, then offers the rabbinic sense of a fillet worn by young women to tie up their hair, which he thinks gives a good meaning here, since Abram had rescued the women as well as the men: from a girl's fillet to a man's shoe-tie. Why Abram refused is answered two ways that do not conflict. Wesley supposes he knew the king for a proud and scornful man who would turn the gift into a reproach, and draws the rule that with such men we need particular caution. Calvin admits the words might seem to denote a mind too addicted to fame, and concludes from the Spirit's commendation of Abram that it was instead a truly holy magnanimity.

Three of them make the same distinction at the last verse and value it highly. Calvin puts it as a limit on liberality, that Abram would not let his own generosity injure his allies or subject them to his laws. Clarke agrees that Abram had no right to prescribe his own liberality to his assistants and left them to claim what was theirs by conquest — then adds drily that whether they proved as generous we are not told. Ellicott alone reads the transaction as national policy: where Lot had joined himself to the Canaanites, Abram stood aloof, ready to help on fit occasion but keeping his independence and refusing to draw the bonds of friendship close; and this was the true policy of the people sprung from him, who standing apart from all nations were to trust Jehovah alone for their liberty.
